messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cashier
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arthur presents as a quiet, stoic man, his 76 years etched into the deep lines around his eyes. He has worked as a cashier at a small neighbourhood grocery store for the past decade, a job he took after his wife, Eleanor, passed. The trauma that brings him to therapy, however, is far older, rooted in a life he left behind in Europe fifty years ago. He speaks of it in a flat, distant tone, as if narrating a story about a stranger. He can describe the precise colour of the sky and the make of the car, a small, rattling sedan he was driving with Eleanor beside him. But when he recounts the ambush on that country road—the sudden eruption of gunfire, the shattering of the passenger-side window—he feels nothing at all. This detached recall, where the memory unfolds like a silent film, is a stark contrast to how the event lives in his body day to day.

The trauma rarely returns as a full narrative. Instead, it is a series of stark, intrusive images that ambush him without warning. It is the spiderweb of cracks spreading across the glass, or the bright, impossible red blooming on Eleanor’s sleeve. These visual memories are so potent that for a moment, he feels he is right back in that car, the engine stalled and the smell of cordite in the air. This terrifying sense of reliving the event immediately ignites a profound sense of threat. His heart hammers in his chest, and the quiet aisles of the grocery store suddenly feel menacing. In these moments, he is certain that the world is a fundamentally dangerous place, a conviction that has calcified over the decades. He finds himself watching customers with an intensity that unnerves them, tracking their hands and their movements, constantly on guard for the first sign of harm.

This ever-present sense of threat has, over time, reshaped his life into a series of careful negotiations with fear. The most significant of these is his absolute refusal to get behind the wheel of a car, or even be a passenger. The intrusive images are most powerful there, and the feeling of being trapped inside a metal box is unbearable. This avoidance, born from the terror of his memories, has become a cage. His daughter, who lives two towns over, has begged him to visit his grandchildren, but the thought of the car journey makes him physically ill. This strategy of avoidance only serves to strengthen the original memory; with no new, safe experiences in a vehicle, the ambush remains his only salient reference point. The avoidance also feeds his hypervigilance. Because he feels safest at home, the world outside becomes, by definition, more threatening, justifying his need to remain super-alert and watchful.

His world has shrunk to the small radius he can walk, a reality that has profoundly eroded his sense of self. He looks at his life and sees a man who cannot do the simple things others take for granted, confirming his deeply held belief that he is no longer the capable, strong person who once built a new life for his family. This appraisal, in turn, makes the traumatic memories more accessible; feeling weak and helpless in the present primes him to recall the ultimate moment of helplessness from his past. The strategies he uses to manage his fear have become a feedback loop of despair. He spends long hours wondering why this happened to him, a circular quest for meaning that only deepens his conviction that he has lost his faith in any kind of benevolent order to the world. He actively pushes away moments of joy or contentment, finding them dissonant and unsafe; feeling good is a luxury he cannot afford, a lowering of the guard that might invite disaster.

The constant vigilance is utterly exhausting. At night, he lies awake for hours, unable to sleep because his body remains on high alert, listening for any sound that might signal danger. This chronic state of threat has cemented his negative appraisals of the world. After decades of feeling unsafe, he has come to believe that people are fundamentally untrustworthy and that life is little more than a series of potential ambushes. It was his daughter’s tearful ultimatum—that if he could not find a way to come to them, he might lose touch with his grandchildren altogether—that finally brought him to seek help. Arthur fears he is running out of time, that he will die in his small apartment, a prisoner of a single afternoon fifty years ago, forever watching the world for a threat that has already come and gone.
